summary.en: Mainstream stars such as the Rolling Stones, Jimi Hendrix, and Eric Clapton were not the main force of the psychedelic wave, but they still contributed to its development.
summary.zh: The Rolling Stones、Jimi Hendrix、Eric Clapton等主流明星并非迷幻风潮的主力，但对其发展亦有贡献。

body.zh:
The Rolling Stones、Jimi Hendrix、Eric Clapton等主流明星并非迷幻风潮的主力，但对其发展亦有贡献。

在上一节中，我们讲到了伦敦的地下（迷幻）场景，以及与之密切关联、但在商业上不那么成功的乐队；即使这些乐队取得了成功，也仅限于英国本土。

接下来就说说参与了迷幻风潮的主流艺人。我们曾经提到the Beatles，包括他们如何走出英国，如何在60年代末开展自己的事业。再来看看the Rolling Stones吧，或许你们不同意，但我还是认为在60年代——至少在68或69年之前——the Rolling Stones就像是Beatles的跟班。The Beatles首先在国际上取得了巨大成功，而the Rolling Stones追随其后。这两个乐队关系不错，我不想说the Stones待在the Beatles的影子里，因为前者真的很成功；但从很多方面来看，the Rolling Stones真正走上自己的路，就是在和the Beatles分道扬镳之后。从此开始，他们就真的成了独一无二的乐队。他们在1967年12月发表的专辑是个很好的例子，它收到的反响非常好，在美国排名第2位、在英国排名第3位。这张专辑叫做《Their Satanic Majesties Request》，常被视为the Rolling Stones 对《Sgt. Pepper》的回应。很多评论人不喜欢它，但你可以有自己的看法。它的封面很棒，是一张全息图，乐队成员都戴着巫师帽。这张图看起来是三维的，在当时真的算是高科技了。有趣的是，就连the Rolling Stones自身也觉得应该对《Sgt. Pepper》作出回应。由此，你可以看出两个乐队之间的关系。 The Beatles的《Magical Mystery Tour》遭遇失败，我认为这在某种程度上让the Rolling Stones松了一口气。这解放了他们。1968年的专辑《Beggar's Banquet》，例如其中的《Street Fighting Man》《Sympathy for the Devil》等曲目，真正突破了追随the Beatles的模式。这才是我们认知中的在70年代发展成型的the Rolling Stones。同期，他们发行了单曲《Jumpin' Jack Flash》，在美国排名第3位，英国排名第1位。从那个时候开始，你可以看到the Rolling Stones自己开创的风格，其并非十分迷幻。但是，《Their Satanic Majesty's Request》以及某些单曲如《She's a Rainbow》，确实融入了迷幻美学。到了68年，他们脱离了这种风格，就跟the Beatles 一样。

然后来聊聊Jimi Hendrix与Eric Clapton，也即the Jimi Hendrix Experience和Cream这两个乐队。他们基本是同一种路数——布鲁斯加上迷幻。Clapton和Hendrix之所以重要，是因为他们共同在摇滚乐领域里发扬了“技艺精湛”的概念，也即不仅要唱得好、歌本身写得好，弹得如何也十分关键。有时候吉他solo甚至可以比演唱更重要，没人想过摇滚吉他手能够创造出那么好的音乐。这就是Clapton与Hendrix在1966到1969年间打造的“吉他英雄”的概念。

稍微讲讲Jimi Hendrix吧，他生于西雅图——我们谈过Hendrix在伦敦场景崭露头角的经历，但他是西雅图人——Hendrix跟着很多R&B乐队在美国巡回演出，与Little Richard和the Isley Brothers等人合作。Jimi与Little Richard之间有个故事广为流传，即Jimi被后者踢出乐队的原因是他夺走了人们对Little Richard的关注。Little Richard告诉他，舞台上只能有一个主角，那就是我。于是Hendrix只能离开。但等到Hendrix在纽约Greenwich Village的Cafe Wha演出时，他已是一个经验丰富的乐手了；在那里演奏时，他引起了the Animals的贝斯手Chas Chandler的注意。当时Chas正考虑转行当经纪人，于是提出他可以为Jimi服务，只要后者愿意搬到伦敦发展，因为他所有的人脉都在伦敦。Jimi对此很感兴趣，并对Chas Chandler说，我非常愿意这么做，前提是你答应把我介绍给Eric Clapton。现在没人知道这个故事是不是后来编造的，但至少人们都这么传说。我讲这个故事，是为了向大家表明 Jimi Hendrix和Eric Clapton之间的惺惺相惜。他们都非常欣赏对方的表演，彼此是友好竞争的关系，这种关系也使他们获益匪浅。稍后我们会聊到这件事。再来看看the Jimi Hendrix Experience乐队的成员，Mitch Mitchell任鼓手，Noel Redding任贝斯手——尽管他之前没当过贝斯手，基本是弹原声吉他的民谣歌手。《Purple Haze》或《Foxy Lady》可能是他们在布鲁斯和流行乐方面的典范之作，另有一些更实验、更迷幻的作品如《If 6 was 9》《1983…(A Merman I Should Turn To Be)》。他们一起制作的三张专辑中，既有传统的布鲁斯，也有类似电台热播单曲那种偏流行的布鲁斯，还有实验性的东西，那种在迷幻风潮中常见的将录音棚本身当成乐器使用的做法。

接下来说说Cream和Eric Clapton。Cream成立于1966年7月，成员包括当时已被誉为英国最佳吉他手之一的Clapton，担任贝斯手兼主唱的Jack Bruce，以及担任鼓手的Ginger Baker。这支乐队自始就被当作超级乐队，尽管Clapton的光环有些盖过了另外两人。他们采纳了很多传统布鲁斯的元素，实际上，Eric Clapton是传统布鲁斯的拥趸。这挽救了很多几乎为人忘却的音乐家。他们翻唱过Robert Johnson的歌曲如《Crossroads Blues》，也翻唱过Muddy Waters的歌曲如《Rollin’ and Tumblin’》；这些曲目以Eric连续不断的solo为特点，在歌曲收尾时进行大段solo也成了他们与The Yardbirds表演时的惯例，此被称为“躁起来“ (rave ups) 。现场版的《Spoonful》（Wille Dixon原唱) 就是一个好例子。Jack Bruce也会为歌曲带来流行的元素，可见于流行单曲如《I Feel Free》《Strange Brew》。

如果把Cream和Hendrix Experience的6张专辑放到一块，就不难发现它们是交错发表的。 Cream的专辑先行一步，the Jimi Hendrix Experience追随其后。依照发表顺序来听这些专辑，可以从中看出他们不断蓬勃的野心，试验着录音室的可能性以及各类演奏技巧。最初是1966年12月的《Fresh Cream》，1967年5月的《Are You Experienced？》与之呼应；67年11月《Disraeli Gears》发表，《Axis Bold as Love》于同年12月发表；然后是68年6月Cream的《Wheels of Fire》，Hendrix则在10月推出《 Electric Ladyland》。这个序列非常整齐。但凡听听以上专辑中的一张，你就能理解体会到何为“吉他英雄”，这个时至今日依然受到致敬的传统。一切都归功于这两个家伙。再次重申，这些都是大众视野中的事情，尽管从很多方面来说，等到Hendrix参加Monterey音乐节并在美国巡回演出后，美国观众才重新认识了他。起初，他在英国比在美国成功得多。

以下是其他值得一提的牵涉迷幻风格的英国主流艺人。首先是Traffic乐队。Stevie Winwood离开the Spencer Davis Group之后加入了他们，其有一首排名第5的热门，叫做《Paper Sun》，是一首很美的流行迷幻歌曲。然后是Van Morrison。在Them乐队时，他们录制了一首名为《Gloria》的经典曲目；但在成为独唱艺人后，他发表的《Brown Eyed Girl》就不怎么迷幻了。他在1968年发表的专辑《Astral Weeks》被视为代表作，对歌迷而言尤其如此。至于Donovan，在60年代中期曾被视为英格兰版本的Bob Dylan。他唱过一些比较古怪的流行单曲，例如1966年的《Sunshine Superman》，美国排名第1位；《Mellow Yellow》，在美国排名第2位。最具迷幻色彩的民谣歌曲大概也是出自他的手，即1969年的《Atlantis》。它在美国榜单上排名第7位，讲述了关于失落之城“亚特兰蒂斯”的故事。关于Donovan的另一个逸闻是，在 Jimmy Page和John Paul Jones还未组建Led Zeppelin时，他们都参与了Donovan作品的录制。我认为，Donovan有那么一首歌曲集齐了Led Zeppelin的大部分成员，除了Robert Plant。

那么，我们对当时的伦敦场景有了初步的了解。但伦敦和旧金山并非迷幻乐的全部领地，在下一节中，我们将研究洛杉矶和其余地方的情况。
body.en:
Mainstream stars such as the Rolling Stones, Jimi Hendrix, and Eric Clapton were not the main force of the psychedelic wave, but they still contributed to its development.

Last section we covered London’s underground (psychedelic) scene and bands closely tied to it but less successful commercially—or successful only in Britain.

Now mainstream artists who took part in the psychedelic wave. We have already mentioned the Beatles—how they left Britain and built their late-1960s career. Look at the Rolling Stones: you may disagree, but I still think that in the 1960s—at least before 1968 or 1969—the Stones were like the Beatles’ followers. The Beatles first won huge international success; the Stones followed. The bands got along; I do not want to say the Stones stayed in the Beatles’ shadow, because they were truly successful; but in many ways the Stones found their own path only after parting ways with the Beatles’ model. From then on they became a unique band. Their December 1967 album is a good example: strong response, No. 2 in the U.S., No. 3 in Britain. Their Satanic Majesties Request is often seen as the Stones’ answer to Sgt. Pepper. Many critics disliked it; you can decide for yourself. The cover is great—a hologram, band members in wizard hats, looking three-dimensional; high tech for the time. Interestingly, even the Stones felt they should answer Sgt. Pepper. That shows the relationship between the two bands. The Beatles’ Magical Mystery Tour flop, I think, somewhat relieved the Stones. It freed them. 1968’s Beggars Banquet—tracks like “Street Fighting Man” and “Sympathy for the Devil”—truly broke the follow-the-Beatles pattern. That is the Rolling Stones we know as they take shape in the 1970s. In the same period they released “Jumpin’ Jack Flash,” No. 3 in the U.S., No. 1 in Britain. From then you see the Stones’ own style—not very psychedelic. But Satanic Majesties and singles like “She’s a Rainbow” did take in psychedelic aesthetics. By 1968 they left that style, as the Beatles did.

Then Jimi Hendrix and Eric Clapton—the Jimi Hendrix Experience and Cream. Same basic path: blues plus psychedelia. Clapton and Hendrix matter because together they advanced “virtuosity” in rock: not only singing and writing well, but how you play. Sometimes a guitar solo could matter more than the vocal; no one had thought rock guitarists could make music that good. That is the “guitar hero” idea Clapton and Hendrix built between 1966 and 1969.

A little on Jimi Hendrix: born in Seattle—we covered how he emerged in the London scene, but he was a Seattleite—he toured the U.S. with many R&B bands, working with Little Richard and the Isley Brothers. A well-known story: Little Richard kicked him out because he stole the spotlight. Little Richard told him there could be only one star on stage—me. So Hendrix left. By the time he played Cafe Wha? in New York’s Greenwich Village he was already a seasoned player; there he caught the eye of the Animals’ bassist Chas Chandler. Chandler was thinking of becoming a manager and offered to work with Jimi if he would move to London, where Chandler’s contacts were. Jimi was interested and told Chandler he would—if Chandler introduced him to Eric Clapton. No one knows if the story was invented later, but that is how people tell it. I tell it to show the mutual regard between Hendrix and Clapton. Each admired the other’s playing; friendly rivalry that helped both. We will come back to that. In the Experience: Mitch Mitchell on drums, Noel Redding on bass—though he had not been a bassist before, mostly an acoustic folk singer. “Purple Haze” or “Foxy Lady” may be models of their blues-and-pop side; more experimental psychedelic pieces include “If 6 Was 9” and “1983… (A Merman I Should Turn to Be).” Across their three albums together you get traditional blues, radio-hit-style pop blues, and experimental work that treats the studio itself as an instrument—common in the psychedelic wave.

Now Cream and Eric Clapton. Cream formed in July 1966: Clapton, already among Britain’s best guitarists; Jack Bruce on bass and vocals; Ginger Baker on drums. It was treated as a supergroup from the start, though Clapton’s aura somewhat overshadowed the others. They took in much traditional blues; Clapton was a traditional-blues devotee. That rescued many nearly forgotten musicians. They covered Robert Johnson’s “Cross Road Blues,” Muddy Waters’ “Rollin’ and Tumblin’”; tracks featured Eric’s continuous solos, and long closing solos became routine from Yardbirds days—“rave-ups.” The live “Spoonful” (Willie Dixon) is a good example. Jack Bruce also brought pop elements, as in hits like “I Feel Free” and “Strange Brew.”

Put Cream’s and the Experience’s six albums together and you see them released interleaved. Cream first, then Hendrix following. Hearing them in release order shows growing ambition—studio possibilities and playing technique. First Fresh Cream (December 1966), answered by Are You Experienced (May 1967); November 1967 Disraeli Gears, December Axis: Bold as Love; then June 1968 Cream’s Wheels of Fire, October Hendrix’s Electric Ladyland. A very neat sequence. Hear any one of these and you understand “guitar hero,” a tradition still honored today. All thanks to these two. Again: this was in public view, though in many ways America only rediscovered Hendrix after Monterey and his U.S. tours. At first he was far more successful in Britain than in America.

Other British mainstream artists worth mentioning for psychedelic style. First Traffic: after Stevie Winwood left the Spencer Davis Group he joined them; they had a No. 5 hit, “Paper Sun,” a beautiful pop-psychedelic song. Then Van Morrison: with Them he cut the classic “Gloria”; as a solo artist “Brown Eyed Girl” is not very psychedelic. His 1968 album Astral Weeks is seen as a landmark, especially by fans. Donovan, in the mid-1960s, was treated as England’s Bob Dylan. He had some odd pop singles—“Sunshine Superman” (1966) No. 1 in the U.S.; “Mellow Yellow” No. 2. His most psychedelic folk song is probably 1969’s “Atlantis,” No. 7 in the U.S., about the lost city of Atlantis. Another Donovan anecdote: before Jimmy Page and John Paul Jones formed Led Zeppelin, both played on Donovan sessions. I think Donovan has one song that gathers most of Led Zeppelin except Robert Plant.

So we have a first look at the London scene. But London and San Francisco were not all of psychedelia; next we look at Los Angeles and elsewhere.
